An index in which each item’s price change is multiplied by its share of total expenditure (or trade value) before summing.
The theory that the prices of primary commodities tend to fall over the long run relative to manufactured goods, so the terms of trade of primary exporters deteriorate.
Damage to other export sectors when a resource boom causes the currency to appreciate, making manufactures and services less competitive.
A long period, often lasting a decade or more, of rising and then falling commodity prices driven by sustained changes in world demand.

diagrams.title: Rising world demand for a commodity export
diagrams.caption: Supply is price inelastic in the short run, so a rise in demand (D1 to D2) causes a large rise in price (P1 to P2) and only a small rise in quantity. Export prices rise relative to import prices, so the copper exporter’s terms of trade improve.

diagrams.title: Terms of trade of a primary exporter over time (illustrative)
diagrams.caption: The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis predicts a long-run downward trend in a primary exporter’s terms of trade, with large short-run fluctuations around it caused by commodity price cycles.

formulae.name: Terms of trade index
formulae.formula: (Index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100
formulae.example: Export prices 112, import prices 128: ToT = 112 ÷ 128 × 100 = 87.5, a 12.5% deterioration from the base of 100.

formulae.name: Weighted price index
formulae.formula: Σ (weight × price index of each item)

applications: UK 2022: as a net importer of gas, the UK suffered a sharp deterioration in its terms of trade when wholesale gas prices soared after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Bank of England described the result as a large real income shock: the UK had to export more to pay for the same energy imports, so real wages and household incomes fell while CPI inflation peaked at around 11%.

UK 2016: the depreciation of sterling after the EU referendum raised import prices in pounds more than export prices, worsening the UK’s terms of trade and pushing CPI inflation up to around 3% by late 2017, squeezing real wages.

Norway: the same 2022 energy price rise sharply improved Norway’s terms of trade, generating record government revenue, much of which was saved in its sovereign wealth fund to avoid Dutch disease and smooth spending for future generations.

Zambia and Chile: as major copper exporters, their terms of trade, export revenue and exchange rates move closely with the copper price. The 2000s China-driven boom improved their terms of trade; falls in copper prices in 2015 contributed to a sharp depreciation of the Zambian kwacha and to Zambia’s debt difficulties, culminating in a default in 2020.

Electric vehicles and the energy transition: rising demand for lithium, cobalt and copper improved the terms of trade of producers such as Chile, Australia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, though lithium prices then fell sharply as supply expanded, showing the volatility of commodity-based terms of trade.
evaluation: An improvement is only beneficial if it reflects stronger demand for exports. If it reflects higher relative inflation or an appreciation and demand is price elastic, export revenue falls and the current account and employment worsen.

Price elasticity of demand for exports and imports determines the effect on the current account. For commodities with inelastic demand, a price fall cuts export revenue sharply; for manufactures with elastic demand, a price fall can raise revenue.

Time period: short-run commodity price spikes may reverse quickly, so governments should not treat windfall revenue as permanent. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund is a model of prudent management; many resource exporters have instead suffered boom-bust cycles.

Size of the trade sector: a change in the terms of trade matters far more for a very open economy, or one dependent on a single commodity, than for a large diversified economy where trade is a smaller share of GDP.

Distribution: a commodity boom benefits mining companies and government revenue but may harm manufacturers and farmers through Dutch disease; an import price shock hurts low-income households most because energy and food are a larger share of their spending.
The ToT measure ignores quality changes and volumes, and depends on the base year and weights, so a fall in the index does not by itself show that welfare has fallen.
misconceptions: Calling an improvement in the terms of trade automatically good for the economy. It depends on the cause and elasticities; an improvement due to high inflation can worsen the current account.
Subtracting percentage changes instead of dividing indices. Export prices +5% and import prices +10% give a ToT of 95.5, not 95.
Confusing the terms of trade with the balance of trade. The ToT is a ratio of prices; the balance of trade is the value of exports minus the value of imports.
Confusing a fall in index points with a percentage fall when the starting index is not 100.

Thinking a depreciation improves the terms of trade. A depreciation lowers export prices in foreign currency and raises import prices in domestic currency, so the terms of trade deteriorate (even though competitiveness improves).
exam_tips: Calculation questions (4–5 marks) are common: write the formula, substitute the numbers, give the answer to one decimal place and state whether it is an improvement or deterioration. Always state the direction in words.
If given export and import price changes for several products, build weighted indices first. Show your weights.
In evaluation, always ask: what caused the change, and what are the price elasticities? This alone usually lifts an answer into the top evaluation band.
Developing economy questions on Paper 2 or 3 often pair the terms of trade with primary product dependency, the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis and diversification strategies (4.3.2, 4.3.3).

model_answer.question: Evaluate the likely impact on a developing economy that depends on copper exports of a significant improvement in its terms of trade caused by rising world demand for copper.
model_answer.answer:
The terms of trade are the ratio of average export prices to average import prices, multiplied by 100. An improvement means each unit of exports buys more imports. For a copper exporter such as Zambia, where copper dominates export earnings, a rise in world copper prices would raise the export price index and improve the terms of trade significantly.

The rise in world demand shifts demand from D1 to D2. Because supply is price inelastic in the short run (new mines take years to develop), price rises substantially from P1 to P2 while quantity rises only a little. Export revenue therefore rises strongly. This improves the current account and earns foreign currency that can be used to import capital goods such as machinery, which developing economies often cannot produce themselves. Government revenue from royalties and corporation tax on mining firms rises, which can fund infrastructure, education and health, raising human capital and long-run productivity, shifting LRAS to the right.

Higher export revenue also raises aggregate demand directly through (X − M), with a multiplier effect as mine workers and suppliers spend their higher incomes. Real GDP and employment rise. Because the terms of trade have improved, real national income rises by more than real GDP: the same volume of exports buys more imports, so living standards improve.

However, there are significant risks. First, the improvement may be temporary. Commodity prices are highly volatile, and if the government treats a windfall as permanent, increasing current spending and borrowing, a later fall in copper prices can cause a fiscal crisis. Zambia's experience after copper prices fell in 2015, followed by a debt default in 2020, illustrates this.

Second, Dutch disease. Increased demand for the currency to buy copper exports causes an appreciation. This makes other exports, such as agricultural products and manufactures, less price competitive, and cheaper imports compete with domestic firms. The economy becomes even more dependent on copper, increasing its vulnerability.

Third, distribution and governance. Mining is capital intensive and often foreign-owned, so profits may be repatriated and few jobs created. Revenue may be captured by elites or lost through corruption rather than invested, so the impact on development may be small.

Finally, the long-run Prebisch-Singer hypothesis suggests that primary commodity prices tend to fall relative to manufactures because of their low income elasticity of demand, so a single improvement does not change the structural problem.

The overall impact depends mainly on how the windfall is managed. If the government saves part of it in a stabilisation or sovereign wealth fund, as Chile and Norway have done, and invests the rest in diversification and human capital, the improvement can raise living standards sustainably. If it is spent on current consumption and the currency appreciates sharply, the short-term boost to growth and the current account is likely to be followed by a painful bust. On balance, the effect is likely to be strongly positive in the short run, but whether it is positive in the long run depends on governance and diversification.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: correct definition and understanding that the cause of the improvement matters. Application: relevant use of copper, Zambia, Chile and Norway, and the inelastic supply diagram. Analysis: chains to export revenue, the current account, AD and the multiplier, government revenue and LRAS, and real national income. Evaluation: temporary versus permanent change, Dutch disease, distribution and governance, Prebisch-Singer, and a conditional judgement that identifies the decisive factor. Top level for a 15-mark question.

check.q: A country’s export price index rises from 100 to 120 and its import price index rises from 100 to 150. Its terms of trade index is now:
check.explanation: ToT = (120 ÷ 150) × 100 = 80, a 20% deterioration.

check.q: Which of the following would improve a country’s terms of trade?
options: Depreciation of its currency
Rise in world prices of its main import
Appreciation of its currency
Faster productivity growth in its export industries
check.explanation: An appreciation raises export prices in foreign currency and lowers import prices in domestic currency, so the ratio of export to import prices rises.

check.q: A country’s terms of trade improve because its inflation is higher than its trading partners’. If demand for its exports is price elastic, the most likely result is:
options: Rise in export revenue
Fall in export revenue and a worse current account
No change in export revenue
Rise in export volumes
check.explanation: Higher relative prices with elastic demand cause a proportionately larger fall in export volumes, so export revenue falls and the current account worsens.

check.q: The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis is based mainly on the fact that:
options: Manufactured goods have a lower income elasticity of demand than primary products
Primary products have a lower income elasticity of demand than manufactured goods
Primary products have more elastic supply
Manufactured goods face higher tariffs
check.explanation: As world incomes rise, demand for manufactures grows faster than demand for primary products, so the relative price of primary products tends to fall over time.

check.explanation: (99 − 110) ÷ 110 × 100 = −10%. The fall is 11 index points but 10 per cent.

title: Trading blocs and the WTO
overview: Trading blocs are groups of countries that reduce barriers to trade among themselves, ranging from free trade areas to full monetary unions. This topic asks you to distinguish the types of bloc, analyse their costs and benefits using trade creation and trade diversion, evaluate monetary union (the eurozone is the key case), and explain the role of the WTO and the tension between regional deals and multilateral free trade. Brexit, the UK’s new trade deals and the paralysis of the WTO’s dispute system make this a rich topic for current application.
objectives: Distinguish free trade areas, customs unions, common markets and monetary unions, with examples.
Use a diagram to analyse trade creation and trade diversion and their welfare effects.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of regional trade agreements for members and non-members.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of monetary union and the conditions for its success.
Explain the role of the WTO in trade liberalisation and dispute settlement.
Analyse possible conflicts between regional trade agreements and the WTO.

sections.heading: Types of trading bloc: a ladder of integration
sections.body:
Each type of bloc includes the features of the one before it.

- **Free trade area (FTA).** Members remove tariffs and quotas on trade with each other, but each sets its own tariffs on non-members. Because external tariffs differ, FTAs need **rules of origin** to stop goods entering through the member with the lowest tariff and being re-exported. Examples: USMCA (US, Mexico, Canada), EFTA, the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (zero tariffs on goods that meet rules of origin), and the UK's FTAs with Australia and New Zealand.
- **Customs union.** An FTA plus a **common external tariff** (CET) on imports from outside. No rules of origin are needed internally, so goods circulate without customs checks on origin, but members give up an independent trade policy: they negotiate trade deals as one. Examples: the EU customs union; Mercosur (in principle).
- **Common market (single market).** A customs union plus **free movement of factors of production** (labour and capital) and common regulations and standards to remove non-tariff barriers. The EU single market's 'four freedoms' cover goods, services, capital and people.
- **Monetary union.** A common market with a **single currency** and a single central bank setting one monetary policy. The eurozone, with the European Central Bank, is the main example. Full **economic union** would add closely coordinated or common fiscal policy.

As integration deepens, the potential gains from trade rise, but so does the loss of national sovereignty over trade, regulatory, migration and eventually monetary policy. Brexit was a decision to move from the common market stage to a (relatively thin) FTA.

sections.heading: Trade creation and trade diversion
sections.body:
Viner's analysis shows that a customs union has two opposing static effects. Use the diagram: domestic demand D and domestic supply S for a good, a world price Pw (the lowest-cost producer outside the bloc, perfectly elastic supply), a tariff that raises the import price to Pw+t, and a partner country whose price Pp is above Pw but below Pw+t.

**Before joining**, imports come from the cheapest world producer at Pw+t. Domestic output is 4 units, consumption 6, imports 2. The government earns tariff revenue (Pw+t − Pw) × imports.

**After joining**, partner goods enter tariff-free at Pp, which is cheaper than world goods plus the CET. Price falls to Pp, domestic output falls to 3, consumption rises to 7, and imports rise to 4, now all from the partner.

- **Trade creation** is the replacement of higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost partner imports (the production triangle) and the extra consumption made possible by the lower price (the consumption triangle). Both are welfare gains.
- **Trade diversion** is the switch from the cheapest world supplier to a higher-cost partner. The original imports now cost Pp to produce instead of Pw. The rectangle (Pp − Pw) × original imports was previously tariff revenue; it is now a pure resource cost. It is a welfare loss.

In the diagram, each triangle has area 0.5 (total 1) while the diversion rectangle has area 2, so joining reduces welfare. Whether a bloc raises welfare depends on the relative sizes, so it is more likely to be beneficial when:

- the partner is a low-cost producer (Pp close to Pw), so diversion is small;
- pre-union tariffs were high, so trade creation is large;
- demand and domestic supply are price elastic, so the triangles are large;
- members were already major trading partners.

There are also **dynamic** effects: larger markets allow economies of scale, increased competition improves efficiency, and blocs attract FDI from firms wanting to sell inside the CET (for example Japanese car makers setting up in the UK from the 1980s to access the EU market).

sections.heading: Costs and benefits of regional trade agreements
sections.body:
**Benefits for members**

- Trade creation: lower prices and more choice for consumers.
- Dynamic gains: economies of scale, competition, innovation and technology spillovers.
- Increased FDI from outside firms seeking tariff-free access.
- Greater bargaining power in negotiations with other large economies (the EU negotiates as one of the world's largest markets).
- Political cooperation and stability.
- In common markets, labour mobility fills skills shortages and capital flows to the most productive uses.

**Costs for members**

- Trade diversion away from lower-cost world producers.
- Loss of sovereignty: members cannot set their own tariffs or sign independent trade deals in a customs union, and must accept common rules in a single market.
- Adjustment costs and structural unemployment in industries exposed to partner competition.
- Regional inequality if activity concentrates in the core of the bloc.
- Costs of contributions to bloc budgets and common policies.

**Costs for non-members**: lost export markets due to trade diversion, and possibly lower world prices for their exports. Developing countries are especially affected by agricultural protection inside blocs such as the EU's Common Agricultural Policy.

**Brexit as a test case.** Leaving the EU's single market and customs union gave the UK an independent trade policy (the UK Global Tariff from 2021 and its own trade deals) and control of migration, but raised non-tariff barriers with its largest partner. The OBR assumes long-run UK trade intensity will be around 15% lower and productivity around 4% lower than if the UK had remained, while independent estimates of the gains from new FTAs are much smaller.

sections.heading: Monetary union: costs, benefits and conditions for success
sections.body:
**Benefits**

- No transaction costs of changing currencies.
- No exchange rate uncertainty between members, encouraging trade, cross-border investment and FDI.
- Price transparency, which increases competition.
- A credible, independent central bank may deliver low inflation and lower interest rates, especially for countries with a history of high inflation.

**Costs**

- **Loss of independent monetary policy.** One interest rate is set for the whole union. If one member is in recession while others are booming, the rate will be wrong for at least one of them (one size fits all).
- **Loss of the exchange rate as an adjustment mechanism.** A country that becomes uncompetitive cannot devalue; it must instead cut relative wages and prices ('internal devaluation'), which tends to mean prolonged unemployment.
- **Constraints on fiscal policy**: eurozone rules (deficits below 3% of GDP, debt below 60%) limit counter-cyclical policy.
- **Risk of sovereign debt crises**: a country borrowing in a currency it does not control cannot rely on its own central bank to buy its debt, so markets may demand high interest rates.

The **eurozone crisis** of 2010–12 showed these costs. Greece, Portugal, Ireland, Spain and Cyprus needed bailouts; Greece lost roughly a quarter of its real GDP and unemployment exceeded 25%. Unable to devalue, it had to cut wages and spending. The crisis eased after the ECB promised in 2012 to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.

**Conditions for success (optimal currency area theory)**

- **Synchronised business cycles and similar economic structures**, so that one interest rate suits all members and asymmetric shocks are rare.
- **High labour mobility**, so workers can move from depressed to booming regions.
- **Flexible wages and prices**, so competitiveness can adjust without exchange rate changes.
- **Fiscal transfers**: a central budget that automatically sends money to regions hit by shocks, as within the UK or US.
- **Convergence before entry** in inflation, interest rates, deficits and debt (the Maastricht criteria).

The UK's 'five economic tests' in 2003 concluded the UK was not ready to join the euro, largely because of cyclical and structural differences, particularly in the housing market's sensitivity to interest rates.

sections.heading: The WTO and its role in trade liberalisation
sections.body:
The **World Trade Organization** was established in 1995, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, 1947). It has around 166 members covering the vast majority of world trade.

**Principles**

- **Non-discrimination**: the most-favoured-nation (MFN) principle means a tariff cut offered to one member must be offered to all; national treatment means imported goods must be treated the same as domestic goods once they have entered.
- **Reciprocity and progressive liberalisation** through negotiated rounds.
- **Predictability**: members 'bind' their maximum tariffs.
- Special and differential treatment for developing countries.

**Functions**

- **Negotiating forum.** GATT rounds cut average tariffs on manufactures from very high levels after 1945 to low single digits. The Uruguay Round (1986–94) created the WTO and extended rules to services, agriculture and intellectual property. The Doha Development Round, launched in 2001, has largely stalled, mainly over agricultural subsidies and developing country access.
- **Dispute settlement.** Members can bring cases and, if successful, may be authorised to retaliate. However, the Appellate Body has been unable to function since December 2019 because the US blocked appointments of new judges, so losing parties can 'appeal into the void'. Some members, including the EU, have set up an interim arbitration arrangement.
- **Monitoring** trade policies and providing technical assistance to developing countries.

**Criticisms**: decisions require consensus, so progress is slow; developing countries argue rules favour rich economies (for example agricultural subsidies in the EU and US); and the WTO struggles to discipline large economies such as the US and China, whose 2018–2019 tariff war and the broad US tariffs of 2025 sat uneasily with MFN rules.

sections.heading: Conflicts between regional trade agreements and the WTO
sections.body:
Regional trade agreements (RTAs) breach the MFN principle by definition: members give each other better treatment than outsiders. The WTO permits them (under GATT Article XXIV) if they cover substantially all trade and do not raise barriers to outsiders, but the tensions are real.

- **Trade diversion** harms the lowest-cost producers outside the bloc, contrary to the WTO's goal of efficient global specialisation.
- **The 'spaghetti bowl'**: hundreds of overlapping agreements, each with different rules of origin, raise compliance costs, especially for small firms and developing countries.
- **Reduced incentive for multilateral negotiation**: large economies can get what they want bilaterally, leaving smaller and poorer countries with less bargaining power. The stalling of Doha has coincided with a boom in RTAs.
- **Bloc protectionism**: blocs can use their size to set high external barriers, for example the EU's agricultural protection.

On the other hand, RTAs can be **building blocks** rather than stumbling blocks:

- They liberalise faster than the WTO and in areas it has not reached, such as services, digital trade, investment and regulatory standards.
- They create coalitions that can push multilateral liberalisation and act as laboratories for new rules.
- Growing membership (CPTPP has expanded to include the UK) can gradually approximate wider free trade.

Your judgement should consider whether a particular agreement is open to new members, has low external barriers and liberalises substantially all trade; such agreements are more likely to complement the WTO.

key_terms.definition: A group of countries that remove tariffs and quotas on trade with each other while each keeps its own external tariffs.
A free trade area with a common external tariff on imports from non-members.
A customs union with free movement of factors of production (labour and capital) and common rules to remove non-tariff barriers.
A group of countries sharing a single currency and a single monetary policy set by a common central bank.
An identical tariff that all members of a customs union apply to imports from outside the union.
Rules that define where a product was made, used in free trade areas to decide whether goods qualify for tariff-free treatment.
The replacement of higher-cost domestic production by lower-cost imports from a bloc partner, raising welfare.
The replacement of lower-cost imports from outside a bloc by higher-cost imports from a member, reducing welfare.
The international body, founded in 1995, that sets the rules of world trade, hosts trade negotiations and settles trade disputes between members.
The WTO rule that any trade concession given to one member must be extended to all members.
A region for which a single currency is likely to be beneficial because of synchronised cycles, labour mobility, flexible prices and fiscal transfers.
An economic shock that affects members of a monetary union differently, making a single interest rate inappropriate for some.

diagrams.title: Trade creation and trade diversion in a customs union
diagrams.caption: Before joining, imports Q2–Q3 come from the world at Pw+t. After joining, price falls to the partner price Pp: domestic output falls to Q1 and consumption rises to Q4. The triangles TC are trade creation gains; the rectangle TD is the trade diversion loss from buying from a higher-cost partner instead of the world at Pw.

applications: UK and Brexit: since 1 January 2021 the UK has traded with the EU under an FTA with zero tariffs for goods meeting rules of origin, but outside the customs union and single market. Customs declarations, rules of origin and SPS checks are non-tariff barriers that have particularly affected small exporters and food trade. In 2025 the UK and EU agreed to negotiate an SPS agreement to ease agrifood trade.

UK trade policy: the UK Global Tariff replaced the EU’s common external tariff in 2021, cutting or removing tariffs on many goods. The UK joined the CPTPP (in force for the UK from December 2024), and has FTAs with Australia, New Zealand and India, but government estimates of their GDP gains are small relative to the estimated cost of leaving the single market.

Northern Ireland: to avoid a hard border on the island of Ireland, Northern Ireland follows many EU single market rules for goods. The Windsor Framework (2023) created separate ‘green lane’ and ‘red lane’ arrangements for goods arriving from Great Britain, illustrating the difficulty of combining FTAs, customs unions and borders.

Eurozone: the 2010–12 sovereign debt crisis showed the costs of monetary union without fiscal union. Greece could not devalue, suffered a fall of roughly a quarter in real GDP and unemployment above 25%, and relied on bailouts conditional on austerity.

WTO: the Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since December 2019, weakening enforcement just as US-China tariffs and the 2025 US tariffs tested the MFN principle. Several members, including the EU, use an interim appeal arbitration arrangement instead.

Global blocs: the RCEP, in force from 2022, links 15 Asia-Pacific economies including China, Japan and South Korea; the African Continental Free Trade Area aims to raise low intra-African trade by removing tariffs and harmonising rules.
evaluation: Whether a bloc raises welfare depends on the balance of trade creation and diversion: it is more likely to be beneficial when partners are low-cost producers, pre-union tariffs were high and members already traded heavily.
Static analysis understates the gains: dynamic effects (economies of scale, competition, FDI, innovation) are often larger than the triangles in the diagram, though harder to measure.

Non-tariff barriers matter more than tariffs in modern trade. A deep single market that harmonises standards creates much larger gains than a shallow FTA, which is why Brexit raised UK-EU trade costs despite zero tariffs.
Sovereignty is a trade-off, not purely an economic cost: deeper integration brings larger economic gains but reduces national control over policy. How this is weighed is partly a normative judgement.

Monetary union is most likely to succeed where the optimal currency area conditions hold; the eurozone meets some (high trade integration) but not others (limited labour mobility and fiscal transfers), so its success varies by member.
RTAs and the WTO can be complements or substitutes: open, deep agreements with low external barriers act as building blocks, while closed, protectionist blocs act as stumbling blocks.
misconceptions: Confusing a free trade area with a customs union. Only a customs union has a common external tariff; FTAs need rules of origin because external tariffs differ.
Assuming all extra imports from a partner after joining are trade creation. Imports switched from a cheaper non-member are trade diversion and reduce welfare.
Placing the trade diversion loss in the wrong place on the diagram. It is the rectangle between Pp and Pw for the original volume of imports, which used to be tariff revenue.
Thinking the WTO bans regional trade agreements. They are permitted under Article XXIV if they cover substantially all trade and do not raise external barriers.
Saying the main cost of the euro is ‘higher prices’. The key costs are the loss of independent monetary policy and exchange rate adjustment.
exam_tips: The trade creation/diversion diagram is a high-value diagram for 15 and 25-mark questions on trading blocs. Label Pw, Pw+t, Pp, all four quantities, the two creation triangles and the diversion rectangle.
For monetary union questions, structure the evaluation around the optimal currency area conditions and use the eurozone crisis as evidence.
Be precise with terms: ‘customs union’, ‘single market’ and ‘FTA’ are not interchangeable, and Brexit-related questions reward accurate description of the TCA.
Link to protectionism (4.1.6), exchange rates (4.1.8) and monetary policy (2.6.2, 4.4.3) for synoptic marks.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that regional trading blocs reduce, rather than increase, global economic welfare.
model_answer.answer:
A regional trading bloc is a group of countries that reduce barriers to trade among themselves. It may be a free trade area, a customs union with a common external tariff, a common market with free movement of factors, or a monetary union. The question is whether blocs move the world closer to, or further from, the efficient allocation of resources that comparative advantage predicts under free trade.

Blocs can increase welfare through trade creation. Before a country joins a customs union, imports cost the world price plus the tariff, Pw+t. After joining, partner goods enter tariff-free at Pp. The price falls, so higher-cost domestic production (Q1 to Q2) is replaced by cheaper partner imports, and consumption rises from Q3 to Q4. The two triangles labelled TC are net welfare gains: resources are reallocated towards lower-cost producers and consumers enjoy more of the good at a lower price.

Dynamic effects can add further gains. A larger tariff-free market lets firms exploit economies of scale, lowering long-run average costs. Greater competition reduces X-inefficiency and monopoly power. Blocs attract FDI: Nissan's investment in Sunderland in the 1980s was partly to gain tariff-free access to the European market. Common markets also remove non-tariff barriers through common standards, which matter more than tariffs in modern trade.

However, blocs can reduce welfare through trade diversion. Because outsiders still face the common external tariff, a member may switch its imports from the lowest-cost world producer at Pw to a higher-cost partner at Pp. The original imports now cost (Pp − Pw) more per unit in real resources, shown by the rectangle TD, which was formerly tariff revenue. If TD exceeds the two TC triangles, joining reduces welfare. Non-members also lose: their efficient exporters lose markets, which is particularly damaging for developing countries facing agricultural protection such as the EU's Common Agricultural Policy.

Blocs may also harm global welfare by weakening the WTO. Regional agreements breach the most-favoured-nation principle. With hundreds of overlapping agreements, each with its own rules of origin, firms face a costly 'spaghetti bowl', and large economies have less need to make concessions in multilateral negotiations. The stalling of the Doha Round since 2001 has coincided with a surge in regional deals, and developing countries with little bargaining power are left behind.

Evaluation. Whether trade creation outweighs trade diversion depends on circumstances. Diversion is small when partners are already low-cost producers, so Pp is close to Pw; creation is large when pre-union tariffs were high and demand and supply are price elastic. Blocs between countries that already trade heavily with each other, such as the EU, tend to be more trade-creating. Empirical studies of the EU single market generally find substantial net gains for members, and the UK's experience since Brexit, with higher non-tariff barriers reducing trade with its largest partner, suggests that deep integration delivered real benefits.

Second, the static diagram ignores dynamic effects, which are usually larger. Even if TD exceeds TC in a given market, economies of scale, competition and FDI across the whole economy may outweigh it.

Third, the effect on global welfare depends on how open the bloc is. Agreements with low external tariffs, open accession and liberalisation of 'substantially all trade', such as the CPTPP, which has expanded to include the UK, act as building blocks towards wider free trade. Closed blocs with high external barriers act as stumbling blocks.

Finally, the relevant comparison matters. If the realistic alternative to regional deals is not global free trade but stalled WTO negotiations and rising protectionism, as in the current era of US-China tensions and broad US tariffs, then regional blocs probably increase global welfare relative to what would otherwise happen.

In conclusion, trading blocs can reduce global welfare when they divert trade from low-cost outsiders and undermine multilateral rules, but most evidence suggests large, deep blocs between neighbouring economies create more trade than they divert, especially once dynamic effects are included. The view is therefore only correct for closed, protectionist blocs; for open blocs, and given the current weakness of the WTO, they are more likely to increase global welfare.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate definitions of bloc types, trade creation and diversion, MFN. Application: Nissan, CAP, Doha, CPTPP, Brexit and WTO context. Analysis: diagram-based chains for both creation and diversion, dynamic effects, and the effect on the multilateral system. Evaluation: conditions under which creation exceeds diversion, static versus dynamic effects, open versus closed blocs, and the counterfactual, leading to a conditional and justified judgement. This reaches Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

check.q: Which feature distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
options: Free movement of labour
Common external tariff on non-members
Single currency
Zero tariffs between members
check.explanation: Both remove internal tariffs, but only a customs union sets a common external tariff, which removes the need for internal rules of origin.

check.q: After joining a customs union, a country stops importing a good from a low-cost non-member and imports it from a higher-cost member instead. This is:
options: Trade creation
Trade diversion
Dumping
Retaliation
check.explanation: Switching from the lowest-cost world producer to a higher-cost partner because of the common external tariff is trade diversion, a welfare loss.

check.q: Which condition would make a monetary union most likely to succeed?
options: Members have very different business cycles
Labour is highly immobile between members
There is a central budget providing fiscal transfers to regions hit by shocks
Wages are rigid
check.explanation: Fiscal transfers cushion asymmetric shocks when members can no longer use their own interest rate or exchange rate. The other options make a single monetary policy more costly.

check.q: The WTO’s most-favoured-nation principle requires that:
options: Developing countries receive lower tariffs than developed countries
Any tariff reduction given to one member is given to all members
Members must join a regional trading bloc
All members have the same tariff rates
check.explanation: MFN is the non-discrimination rule: trade concessions to one member must be extended to all. Regional agreements are a permitted exception.

check.q: In the trade creation/diversion diagram, the trade diversion loss is best shown by:
options: The triangle between the supply curve, Pp and Pw+t
The rectangle between Pp and Pw for the volume of pre-union imports
The triangle between the demand curve, Pp and Pw+t
The whole area of tariff revenue
check.explanation: The original imports now cost Pp instead of Pw to produce, so (Pp − Pw) × original imports is a real resource cost. The rest of the old tariff revenue passes to consumers via the lower price.

title: Restrictions on free trade
overview: Protectionism means restricting imports or favouring domestic producers, using tariffs, quotas, subsidies and a wide range of non-tariff barriers. Edexcel expects you to explain why governments restrict trade, draw and interpret the tariff, quota and subsidy diagrams with world price and welfare areas, and evaluate the impact on consumers, producers, governments, living standards and equality. With the US tariffs of 2018 and 2025, EU duties on Chinese electric vehicles and the UK’s support for its steel industry, this is one of the most topical areas of the course.
objectives: Explain the economic and non-economic reasons for restricting trade and evaluate their validity.
Draw and analyse a tariff diagram, identifying changes in consumer surplus, producer surplus, tariff revenue and deadweight loss.
Draw and analyse quota and domestic subsidy diagrams and compare them with a tariff.
Explain the main non-tariff barriers with current examples.
Evaluate the impact of protectionism on consumers, producers, governments, living standards and equality.
Reach a justified judgement on whether protection is ever justified.

sections.heading: Why governments restrict trade
sections.body:
Comparative advantage shows that free trade maximises world output, so why do governments restrict it? Learn the arguments and their weaknesses together.

- **Infant industry argument.** New industries cannot reach the economies of scale enjoyed by established foreign rivals. Temporary protection lets them grow until they are competitive. Weakness: governments are poor at picking winners, and 'temporary' protection is often permanent because protected firms lack incentives to become efficient and lobby to keep it (government failure).
- **Protecting jobs and declining industries.** Protection can slow the decline of industries such as steel to give workers time to adjust and avoid regional structural unemployment. Weakness: jobs saved in the protected industry are often outweighed by jobs lost in industries that use its output, and by retaliation.
- **Anti-dumping.** **Dumping** is selling exports at below their domestic price or below cost, often supported by state subsidies, to gain market share. WTO rules allow anti-dumping and countervailing duties; in the UK, the Trade Remedies Authority investigates cases. Weakness: dumping is hard to prove, and cheap imports benefit consumers.
- **Strategic and national security reasons.** Food, energy, defence, semiconductors and medicines may be too important to rely on imports, as the 2022 energy crisis showed. Weakness: 'strategic' can be stretched to cover almost any industry.
- **Correcting a current account deficit.** Restricting imports reduces spending on imports. Weakness: it treats symptoms, invites retaliation and protects inefficiency.
- **Raising government revenue.** Important for low-income countries with narrow tax bases; much less so for the UK.
- **Protecting standards and the environment.** Bans on products that fail safety, food or environmental standards, and carbon border adjustments to prevent carbon leakage.
- **Retaliation and bargaining.** Threatening tariffs to force others to open their markets. Weakness: it risks trade wars where everyone loses.
- **Terms of trade argument.** A large country can use a tariff to push down the world price of its imports. This can benefit the large country at the expense of its trading partners.

sections.heading: Tariffs: the diagram and the welfare effects
sections.body:
A **tariff** is a tax on imports. It may be **ad valorem** (a percentage of value) or **specific** (a fixed amount per unit).

Use the diagram. The country is small, so it is a price taker facing a perfectly elastic world supply at Pw. Under free trade, domestic firms supply Q1, consumers buy Q4, and imports are Q1–Q4. A tariff raises the domestic price to Pw+t. Then:

- Domestic supply rises to Q2 (domestic firms can now compete at the higher price).
- Domestic demand falls to Q3.
- Imports fall to Q2–Q3.

**Welfare effects (letters refer to the shaded areas)**

- **Consumer surplus** falls by a + b + c + d, because consumers pay more and buy less.
- **Producer surplus** rises by a: domestic producers sell more at a higher price.
- **Government** gains tariff revenue c = tariff per unit × imports.
- **Deadweight loss** = b + d. Area b is the **production inefficiency**: units Q1–Q2 are now produced domestically at a higher cost than the world price. Area d is the **consumption loss**: consumers who valued units Q3–Q4 above their world cost no longer buy them.

**Worked example (illustrative, prices in £, quantities in millions).** Pw = £2, tariff = £2, so the domestic price is £4. Domestic supply rises from 2m to 4m; demand falls from 8m to 6m; imports fall from 6m to 2m.

- Area a = ½ × (2 + 4) × 2 = £6m producer surplus gain.
- Area b = ½ × 2 × 2 = £2m.
- Area c = 2 × 2 = £4m tariff revenue.
- Area d = ½ × 2 × 2 = £2m.
- Consumer surplus loss = 6 + 2 + 4 + 2 = £14m; net welfare loss = £4m.

The tariff transfers income from consumers to producers and the government, and destroys £4m of welfare. The deadweight loss is larger the more price elastic domestic demand and supply are.

sections.heading: Quotas and subsidies to domestic producers
sections.body:
**Quotas** are physical limits on the quantity (or value) of a good that can be imported. In the quota diagram, domestic firms supply up to Q1 at the world price; then the quota is filled; above the world price, total supply is domestic supply plus the fixed quota (S + quota). The new equilibrium is where S + quota meets demand.

With the quota set equal to the imports under the tariff, the price, domestic output, consumption and deadweight losses (b and d) are the same as under the tariff. The crucial difference is area c: instead of becoming government revenue, it is **quota rent** earned by whoever holds the import licences, usually foreign exporters or importers, who buy at Pw and sell at the higher domestic price. Quotas therefore usually reduce national welfare by more than an equivalent tariff. They are also less flexible: if demand rises, the whole adjustment falls on price, not on imports. A **tariff-rate quota** combines the two: a low tariff up to a quota and a high tariff beyond it. The UK uses tariff-rate quotas on some steel products as safeguards.

**Subsidies to domestic producers** lower firms' costs, shifting domestic supply from S1 to S2 (down by the subsidy per unit). Because the country is a price taker, the price stays at Pw, so consumers are unaffected: they still buy Q4. Domestic output rises from Q1 to Q2 and imports fall from Q1–Q4 to Q2–Q4.

In the subsidy diagram (illustrative units), the subsidy of £2 per unit on 4m units costs the government £8m. Of this, £6m is a gain in producer surplus (the shaded area 'PS gain') and £2m is a deadweight loss: output Q1–Q2 is produced at a cost above the world price. A subsidy has a smaller deadweight loss than a tariff with the same effect on domestic output, because there is no consumption loss, but it has an **opportunity cost** for taxpayers. Examples: agricultural support, the long-running Airbus-Boeing subsidy dispute at the WTO, and green industrial subsidies such as the US Inflation Reduction Act.

**Export subsidies** go further, paying firms to sell abroad. They can depress world prices and harm producers in other countries, which is why WTO rules prohibit most of them.

sections.heading: Non-tariff barriers
sections.body:
In modern trade, non-tariff barriers (NTBs) are often more important than tariffs, which are now low between most advanced economies.

- **Regulations and product standards.** Food safety, technical and environmental standards that differ between countries raise costs for exporters. The UK and EU ban chlorine-washed chicken and hormone-treated beef, which limits US agricultural exports. Standards may be genuine consumer protection or disguised protectionism.
- **Customs procedures and border checks.** Customs declarations, rules of origin and sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) checks add cost and delay. These are the main post-Brexit barriers for UK-EU trade.
- **Voluntary export restraints (VERs).** An exporter agrees to limit its exports, usually under pressure. Japan restricted car exports to the US and parts of Europe in the 1980s.
- **Embargoes and sanctions.** Complete bans on trade, such as Western sanctions on many Russian exports since 2022.
- **Government procurement** favouring domestic firms ('buy national' rules).
- **Exchange rate policy.** Holding the currency down makes imports dearer and exports cheaper, a form of hidden protection.
- **Domestic content requirements**, requiring a minimum share of local inputs.
- **Licensing and administrative delays**: burdensome paperwork or deliberately slow inspections.

NTBs are hard to measure and challenge at the WTO because many have legitimate purposes. They are also often regressive in impact and opaque, so consumers rarely realise what they pay.

sections.heading: Impact on consumers, producers, governments, living standards and equality
sections.body:
**Consumers** pay higher prices and have less choice and possibly lower quality. Because tariffs on food, clothing and footwear take a larger share of the incomes of poorer households, protection is often **regressive**.

**Domestic producers** in the protected industry gain higher prices, output and profits, and can keep jobs. But **downstream firms** that use the protected good as an input (car makers using steel, for example) face higher costs and lose competitiveness. Exporters may suffer **retaliation**: when the US imposed steel tariffs in 2018, the EU responded with tariffs on US goods such as bourbon whiskey and motorcycles. Protected firms face less competitive pressure, so X-inefficiency and lack of innovation can follow (dynamic inefficiency).

**Foreign producers** lose sales and profits; for developing countries, protection in rich countries (especially of agriculture) can significantly reduce export earnings.

**Governments** gain tariff revenue but bear the cost of subsidies, risk trade disputes, and face lobbying by protected industries, creating a risk of government failure through regulatory capture.

**Living standards** fall overall: the deadweight losses, reduced specialisation and higher prices reduce real incomes. Studies of the 2018 US tariffs found that the cost was borne almost entirely by US importers and consumers, and that the cost per job saved in steel was very high, far above the wage of the jobs protected.

**Equality.** The effects are mixed. Protection may preserve relatively well-paid manufacturing jobs in deprived regions, reducing regional inequality in the short run, but the regressive effect of higher prices on low-income households pushes the other way. Globally, protection by rich countries can widen inequality between rich and poor nations.

**Macroeconomic effects.** Protection may reduce imports and improve the current account in the short run, but retaliation, a stronger currency (as import demand falls) and higher costs often offset this. Tariffs also add to cost-push inflation.

key_terms.definition: Government policies that restrict imports or favour domestic producers over foreign competitors.
A tax on imported goods, either a percentage of value (ad valorem) or a fixed amount per unit (specific).
A physical limit on the quantity or value of a good that can be imported in a given period.
The extra revenue earned by holders of import licences under a quota, equal to (domestic price − world price) × quota.
A payment to domestic producers that lowers their costs and allows them to compete with imports at the world price.
Any restriction on trade other than a tariff, such as quotas, regulations, standards, customs procedures, embargoes or procurement rules.
Selling exports abroad at a price below their domestic price or below the cost of production.
A new domestic industry that cannot yet compete with established foreign producers because it lacks economies of scale and experience.
An agreement by an exporting country to limit the volume of its exports to a particular market.
The imposition of trade barriers in response to barriers imposed by another country, which can escalate into a trade war.
A system where imports up to a set quantity face a low tariff and imports above it face a higher tariff.

diagrams.title: Effects of a tariff
diagrams.caption: The tariff raises the domestic price from Pw to Pw+t. Domestic output rises Q1 to Q2, consumption falls Q4 to Q3 and imports shrink to Q2–Q3. Consumers lose a+b+c+d; producers gain a; the government gains tariff revenue c; b and d are deadweight losses.

diagrams.title: Effects of an import quota
diagrams.caption: A quota of Q2–Q3 (2m units) shifts total supply to S+quota, raising the price to Pq. Output, consumption and deadweight losses b and d match the tariff, but the rectangle becomes quota rent for licence holders rather than government revenue.

diagrams.title: Subsidy to domestic producers
diagrams.caption: A subsidy shifts domestic supply from S1 to S2. Price stays at Pw, so consumption stays at Q4, but domestic output rises from Q1 to Q2 and imports fall to Q2–Q4. The subsidy cost (PS gain + DWL) falls on taxpayers.

formulae.name: Tariff revenue
formulae.formula: Tariff per unit × quantity of imports after the tariff

formulae.name: Deadweight loss of a tariff
formulae.formula: ½ × tariff × rise in domestic output + ½ × tariff × fall in consumption

formulae.name: Cost of a domestic subsidy
formulae.formula: Subsidy per unit × domestic output after the subsidy
formulae.example: £2 × 4m units = £8m, of which £6m is producer surplus gain and £2m deadweight loss.

applications: UK steel: the UK has kept tariff-rate quota safeguards on several steel products, inherited from the EU and since extended, to limit import surges diverted from the US market. In 2025 the government took control of British Steel’s Scunthorpe works through emergency legislation to keep its blast furnaces running, citing national security, showing how strategic arguments are used to justify intervention.

UK Global Tariff: introduced in January 2021 to replace the EU’s common external tariff, it removed tariffs on many goods not produced in the UK and simplified others, lowering costs for consumers and firms using imported inputs, while keeping tariffs on sensitive agricultural products to protect UK farmers.

US tariffs: in 2018 the US imposed 25% tariffs on steel and 10% on aluminium, and tariffs on a wide range of Chinese goods; the EU retaliated with duties on goods including bourbon whiskey and motorcycles. In 2025 the US introduced a baseline 10% tariff on most imports, including from the UK, with higher rates for many countries; a UK-US deal later cut the tariff on a quota of UK car exports.

EU and Chinese electric vehicles: in 2024 the EU imposed countervailing duties on Chinese-made electric vehicles, arguing that state subsidies allowed unfairly low prices. This illustrates the anti-dumping and anti-subsidy arguments and the tension between protecting producers and giving consumers cheaper green technology.

Agricultural protection: the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy and US farm subsidies have long been criticised for depressing world prices and harming farmers in developing countries, one reason the WTO’s Doha Round stalled.
evaluation: Magnitude of the deadweight loss depends on price elasticities of domestic demand and supply: with inelastic demand and supply the triangles are small, but the transfer from consumers to producers is still large.

Short run versus long run: protection may save jobs and smooth structural change in the short run, but in the long run it reduces incentives to innovate and cut costs, lowering productivity and living standards.

Retaliation: the gains to a protected industry can be wiped out if trading partners retaliate against the country’s exporters. A tariff that looks beneficial in isolation can trigger a trade war where all countries lose.

Who bears the cost: evidence from the 2018 US tariffs showed the cost fell largely on domestic importers and consumers, not foreign exporters, and the cost per job saved was very high. Downstream industries may lose more jobs than are saved.

Infant industry and strategic cases can be valid if protection is temporary, targeted and conditional on performance (as in South Korea), but government failure is likely if protection becomes permanent or is captured by lobbying.
Large versus small countries: a large country may improve its terms of trade with a tariff, shifting costs onto foreign producers, which a small price-taking country cannot do.

Alternatives: a subsidy causes less deadweight loss than a tariff for the same output effect, and supply-side policies (training, infrastructure) or targeted support for displaced workers may achieve the goals of protection at a lower cost.
misconceptions: Thinking foreign firms pay the tariff. The importer pays it, and most of it is usually passed on to domestic consumers through higher prices.
Labelling the tariff revenue rectangle as a deadweight loss. It is a transfer to the government; the deadweight losses are the two triangles.
Assuming quotas and tariffs are identical. They can produce the same price and quantity, but quota rent goes to licence holders, often foreign, instead of the government.
Showing a domestic subsidy raising the domestic price. For a small price-taking country the price stays at the world price; output rises and imports fall.
Assuming protection always improves the current account. Retaliation, currency appreciation and higher input costs can offset the fall in imports.
exam_tips: Learn the tariff diagram until you can draw it in under two minutes: label Pw, Pw+t, Q1–Q4 and areas a, b, c, d, and state who gains and loses each area.
Data response questions may give numbers for the world price, tariff and quantities: calculate tariff revenue, the change in imports and the deadweight loss, showing workings.
Use stakeholder analysis (consumers, domestic producers, downstream firms, government, foreign producers, workers) to structure 15 and 25-mark answers.
Top-band evaluation weighs elasticities, retaliation, time period and the alternatives to protection, then judges whether protection is justified in the specific case given.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the case for a government imposing tariffs on imports of steel to protect its domestic steel industry.
model_answer.answer:
A tariff is a tax on imports, raising their price in the domestic market. Steel is a homogeneous product traded at a world price, and many advanced economies, including the UK, face competition from lower-cost producers, some of whom receive state support.

In a small open economy facing a world price Pw, free trade means domestic steelmakers supply Q1 while consumers buy Q4, with imports making up the difference. A tariff raises the domestic price to Pw+t. Domestic output rises to Q2 and employment in steel rises, protecting jobs in places such as Scunthorpe and Port Talbot where steelworks are major employers and where workers are geographically and occupationally immobile. Without protection, closure could cause long-term structural unemployment, with negative multiplier effects on local suppliers and services. Producer surplus rises by area a, improving profitability and possibly funding investment.

There is also a strategic argument. Steel is needed for defence, infrastructure and the energy transition, so a country may wish to keep domestic capacity rather than depend entirely on imports in a crisis. The UK government's decision in 2025 to take control of British Steel's Scunthorpe works to keep its blast furnaces running reflected this concern. In addition, if imports are being dumped, sold below cost because of foreign subsidies or overcapacity, a tariff can be justified as restoring fair competition, which WTO rules allow through anti-dumping and countervailing duties. The tariff also raises revenue for the government, area c.

However, the costs are significant. Consumers of steel, mainly other firms, pay more: consumer surplus falls by a + b + c + d. The deadweight losses b and d represent inefficient domestic production and lost consumption. Because steel is an input into construction, cars, machinery and packaging, higher prices raise costs throughout the economy, reducing competitiveness of downstream industries that employ far more workers than steel itself. Evidence from the 2018 US steel tariffs suggests jobs lost in steel-using industries outweighed those created in steel, and the cost per job saved was very high.

Second, trading partners may retaliate. After the 2018 US tariffs, the EU imposed duties on US exports such as bourbon and motorcycles, harming unrelated industries.

Third, protection reduces the pressure on domestic producers to cut costs and innovate, so X-inefficiency may increase and the industry may never become competitive, requiring protection indefinitely. This is a form of government failure, made more likely by lobbying.

Evaluation. The strength of the case depends first on the reason for the import competition. If imports are cheap because of genuine comparative advantage, a tariff simply preserves an inefficient industry at a cost to the rest of the economy. If they are cheap because of subsidised overcapacity elsewhere, a targeted anti-dumping duty is more justified. Second, it depends on elasticities: if demand for steel is price inelastic, the consumption loss is small, but most of the cost is a transfer from steel users to producers. Third, time period matters: a temporary tariff that buys time for workers to retrain or for producers to switch to lower-carbon electric arc furnaces may be worthwhile, while permanent protection is not.

Finally, alternatives may achieve the same aims at lower cost. A subsidy to domestic producers raises domestic output without raising the price to steel users, so there is no consumption loss, although it costs taxpayers. Regional and retraining policies may protect workers more efficiently than protecting firms. A tariff-rate quota that only bites when imports surge is a less damaging compromise, which is why the UK has used safeguard quotas rather than broad tariffs.

In conclusion, the general case for steel tariffs is weak because the costs to steel users, consumers and exporters usually outweigh the benefits to steel producers. The case is stronger, however, where there is clear evidence of dumping or a genuine national security need, and if protection is temporary and targeted. Even then, a combination of safeguard quotas, anti-dumping duties and direct support for decarbonisation and workers is likely to be more efficient than a broad tariff.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definition of a tariff and understanding of dumping and WTO rules. Application: steel-specific context, Scunthorpe, US 2018 tariffs and EU retaliation, UK safeguard quotas. Analysis: diagram-based analysis of welfare areas, multiplier and structural unemployment chains, downstream effects and dynamic inefficiency. Evaluation: distinguishes causes of import competition, elasticities, time period and alternatives (subsidy, tariff-rate quota, retraining), leading to a nuanced judgement. Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

check.q: A small country imposes a tariff. Which area on the tariff diagram is a transfer to the government rather than a deadweight loss?
options: The production triangle between S, Pw and Pw+t
The rectangle of tariff × imports after the tariff
The consumption triangle between D, Pw and Pw+t
The area above Pw+t and below demand
check.explanation: Tariff revenue (tariff per unit × remaining imports) is transferred from consumers to the government. The two triangles are deadweight losses.

check.q: World price £5, tariff £1. With the tariff, domestic supply is 30 units and demand 50 units. Tariff revenue is:
check.explanation: Imports = 50 − 30 = 20 units; revenue = £1 × 20 = £20.

check.q: Compared with a tariff that reduces imports by the same amount, an import quota is likely to:
options: Raise more government revenue
Lead to a lower domestic price
Transfer the rectangle of extra revenue to licence holders rather than the government
Eliminate deadweight loss
check.explanation: The price and quantities are the same, but the area that would have been tariff revenue becomes quota rent for those holding import licences.

check.q: A subsidy to domestic producers in a small open economy will most likely:
options: Raise the domestic price and reduce consumption
Leave the price unchanged, raise domestic output and reduce imports
Increase imports
Reduce domestic output
check.explanation: The country is a price taker, so the price remains at the world price; lower costs raise domestic output, replacing some imports.

check.q: Which is the strongest economic criticism of the infant industry argument?
options: Infant industries never have economies of scale
Protection may become permanent because firms lack incentives to become efficient
It always causes a current account deficit
It is banned by all trade agreements
check.explanation: Protected firms face less competitive pressure and may lobby to keep protection, so it often outlasts its purpose: a form of government failure.

title: Balance of payments
overview: The balance of payments records all transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world. At AS level (2.1.4) you met the current account; in Theme 4 you need the full structure, including the capital and financial accounts, the causes of current account deficits and surpluses, the policies used to correct imbalances, and the significance of global trade imbalances. The UK, with a persistent current account deficit financed by inflows of foreign capital, is the obvious case study; Germany and China are the classic surplus economies.
objectives: Identify the components of the current, capital and financial accounts and explain why the balance of payments always balances.
Calculate current account balances and express them as a percentage of GDP.
Explain the cyclical and structural causes of current account deficits and surpluses.
Analyse expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing and supply-side policies to correct an imbalance, using AD/AS diagrams.
Evaluate the significance of deficits and surpluses for individual countries and for the global economy.

sections.heading: Structure of the balance of payments
sections.body:
The balance of payments (BoP) has three accounts.

**1. Current account** records flows of income from trade and from overseas assets.

- **Trade in goods** (visible trade): exports minus imports of physical goods such as cars, pharmaceuticals and fuel.
- **Trade in services** (invisible trade): finance, insurance, tourism, education, transport, consultancy.
- **Primary income**: compensation of employees working abroad and, much more important, **investment income**: profits, dividends and interest earned on overseas assets minus those paid to foreign owners of UK assets.
- **Secondary income**: current transfers, such as migrants' remittances, foreign aid and payments to and from international organisations.

**2. Capital account** (small): capital transfers such as debt forgiveness and migrants' transfers of assets, and the purchase or sale of non-produced, non-financial assets such as land for embassies or certain rights.

**3. Financial account** records flows of financial investment:

- **Foreign direct investment (FDI)**: buying a lasting controlling interest in a firm or building a plant abroad.
- **Portfolio investment**: buying shares and bonds without a controlling interest.
- **Other investment**: bank lending and deposits ('hot money' often flows here).
- **Reserve assets**: changes in the central bank's holdings of foreign currency and gold.

**Why it balances.** Every transaction involves an equal and opposite payment. If the UK buys more goods, services and income from abroad than it sells, foreigners end up holding the extra pounds; they use them to buy UK assets (shares, property, bonds, firms) or lend to UK residents. So a **current account deficit is matched by a net inflow on the financial account** (net borrowing from, or sale of assets to, the rest of the world). In practice the figures do not add up exactly, so a **net errors and omissions** item makes the accounts sum to zero.

sections.heading: Calculating and interpreting the current account
sections.body:
**Worked example (illustrative data, £bn).**

- Exports of goods 400; imports of goods 580: **trade in goods balance = −180**
- Exports of services 450; imports of services 290: **trade in services balance = +160**
- Primary income balance = −30
- Secondary income balance = −25
- **Current account balance** = −180 + 160 − 30 − 25 = **−£75bn**
- With nominal GDP of £2,750bn, the deficit is 75 ÷ 2,750 × 100 = **2.7% of GDP**.

Always express imbalances as a **percentage of GDP** when comparing countries or years: a £75bn deficit is large for a small economy but moderate for the UK.

This pattern resembles the UK's: a large deficit on trade in goods, a large surplus on trade in services, and negative income balances. The UK has run a current account deficit in almost every year since the mid-1980s, reaching over 5% of GDP in the mid-2010s. Part of the widening in the 2010s came from the **primary income** balance turning negative as returns on UK investments abroad fell relative to payments to foreign investors in the UK.

**Interpreting a deficit using national accounting.** A current account balance equals the gap between national saving and domestic investment (S − I), plus the government's fiscal position. A current account deficit means a country is investing and consuming more than it produces and saves, and borrowing the difference from abroad. A deficit that finances productive investment (raising future export capacity) is far less worrying than one financing consumption.

sections.heading: Causes of current account deficits and surpluses
sections.body:
Separate **cyclical** causes, which reverse as the economy moves through the cycle, from **structural** causes, which persist.

**Cyclical causes of a deficit**

- **Strong growth of domestic demand.** When incomes rise quickly, spending on imports rises, especially if the marginal propensity to import and the income elasticity of demand for imports are high. UK consumer booms in the late 1980s and mid-2000s widened the deficit.
- **Weak growth in trading partners**, reducing demand for exports (for example eurozone weakness in 2011–13).
- **A temporarily strong currency** or a commodity price shock (higher energy import prices in 2022).

**Structural causes of a deficit**

- **Lack of price competitiveness**: relatively high unit labour costs, low productivity growth or relatively high inflation.
- **Lack of non-price competitiveness**: weaker quality, design, reliability or branding.
- **Deindustrialisation** and a narrow manufacturing base, so many goods must be imported.
- **A persistently overvalued exchange rate**, sometimes because capital inflows (attracted by high interest rates or a safe financial system) push the currency up.
- **Low national savings**: low household saving and large budget deficits mean domestic spending exceeds output.
- **Investment income outflows** when foreigners own a large share of a country's assets.

**Causes of surpluses** are often the mirror image: high household and corporate saving (Germany), export-led growth strategies with an undervalued or managed currency (China in the 2000s), high competitiveness in manufacturing, and natural resource exports (Norway, Saudi Arabia). Germany's surplus reached around 8% of GDP in the mid-2010s, helped by wage restraint and a euro that was weaker than a German currency would have been. China's surplus approached 10% of GDP around 2007 before falling as it rebalanced towards domestic consumption.

sections.heading: Do deficits and surpluses matter?
sections.body:
**A deficit may not be a problem if:**

- It is **small** (under about 3% of GDP is often seen as sustainable) and **temporary** (cyclical).
- It is financed by **long-term FDI** that raises productive capacity, rather than short-term hot money that can leave suddenly.
- It reflects high **investment** rather than consumption.
- The country can borrow in its **own currency** and has credible institutions (true of the UK and US).

**A deficit is a problem if it is large and persistent**, because:

- It reflects a **leakage from the circular flow**: (X − M) is negative, reducing AD, output and employment, especially in manufacturing.
- It must be financed by selling assets or borrowing, so the country's **net international investment position** worsens and future investment income outflows rise.
- It creates **vulnerability to a 'sudden stop'**: if investors lose confidence they withdraw funds, the currency falls sharply and interest rates may have to rise. In 2017 the then Bank of England Governor Mark Carney described the UK as reliant on 'the kindness of strangers'. The sterling sell-off after the September 2022 mini-budget showed how quickly confidence can shift.
- It may signal **structural weakness** in competitiveness and productivity.
- It puts **downward pressure on the exchange rate**, raising import prices and inflation.

**Surpluses can also cause problems**: they mean domestic consumption is lower than it could be; they put upward pressure on the currency; large surpluses can be inflationary; and they invite protectionist retaliation from deficit countries.

**Global trade imbalances.** One country's surplus is another's deficit. In the 2000s, large surpluses in China, Germany and oil exporters were recycled into US and UK financial assets, holding down long-term interest rates (the 'global savings glut'). Many economists believe this cheap credit contributed to the borrowing boom that preceded the 2008 financial crisis. Persistent imbalances also drive trade tensions: US tariffs on China from 2018 and in 2025 were partly justified by the US trade deficit. Adjustment ideally needs action by both sides: deficit countries saving more and surplus countries spending more.

sections.heading: Policies to correct a current account deficit
sections.body:
**1. Expenditure-switching policies** aim to switch spending from foreign to domestic goods.

- **Depreciation or devaluation** of the currency makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. It improves the current account only if the **Marshall-Lerner condition** holds (sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports greater than 1), and typically only after a time lag (the **J-curve**, covered in 4.1.8). It is also inflationary.
- **Protectionism** (tariffs, quotas) raises the price of imports. It risks retaliation, breaches WTO and trade agreement commitments, and protects inefficient firms.

**2. Expenditure-reducing policies** cut total spending, so spending on imports falls.

- **Contractionary fiscal policy** (higher taxes, lower government spending) or **contractionary monetary policy** (higher Bank Rate) shifts AD left from AD1 to AD2. Real output falls and, with a positive marginal propensity to import, imports fall. Lower inflation also improves price competitiveness.
- The cost is lower growth and higher unemployment: it conflicts with other macroeconomic objectives. Higher interest rates may also attract hot money and cause an appreciation, which worsens price competitiveness and partly offsets the effect.

**3. Supply-side policies** tackle structural causes by raising productivity and competitiveness.

- Education and training, infrastructure investment, R&D incentives (such as tax credits), reforms to planning and regulation, and policies to attract FDI.
- They shift LRAS right, lowering unit costs and inflationary pressure and improving both price and non-price competitiveness, so exports rise without sacrificing growth.
- They are the only policies that address the long-run cause, but they take years to work, have uncertain effects and cost public money.

A **surplus** country can be encouraged to rebalance by expanding domestic demand (fiscal expansion, higher wages) or letting its currency appreciate.

applications: UK: the UK has run a current account deficit in almost every year since the mid-1980s. It combines a large goods deficit with a services surplus driven by finance, professional services and creative industries. The deficit is financed by inflows on the financial account, including FDI and purchases of UK property, shares and government bonds.

UK primary income: in the 2010s the UK’s primary income balance moved from surplus to deficit as earnings on UK-owned assets abroad fell relative to payments to foreign owners of UK assets, widening the current account deficit to over 5% of GDP in the mid-2010s.

UK 2022: higher gas prices sharply increased the value of energy imports, worsening the trade balance. The episode also illustrated the vulnerability of a deficit country: after the September 2022 mini-budget, sterling fell to a record low against the dollar and the Bank of England intervened in the gilt market to restore stability.

Germany: persistent current account surpluses of around 6–8% of GDP in the 2010s reflected high saving, wage restraint and competitive manufacturing within a eurozone exchange rate that was weaker than a stand-alone German currency would have been, attracting criticism from the IMF, the EU Commission and the US.

China: its surplus approached 10% of GDP around 2007 as an export-led strategy combined with a managed currency and very high household saving. It later fell as China shifted towards domestic demand, though large manufacturing surpluses have re-emerged in sectors such as electric vehicles, adding to trade tensions.
evaluation: Size, duration and cause matter: a small, cyclical deficit financed by FDI is very different from a large, persistent, structural deficit financed by hot money.
What the deficit finances matters: borrowing to invest in productive capacity can raise future export earnings, while borrowing to fund consumption builds liabilities without raising future income.

Expenditure-switching via depreciation depends on the Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve, and the inflation it causes may erode the competitive gain; protection risks retaliation and is constrained by WTO and trade agreement rules.
Expenditure-reducing policies conflict with growth and employment objectives: they cure the symptom by making the economy poorer, and may be politically unsustainable.
Supply-side policies address root causes and avoid conflicts with other objectives, but take years to work, are uncertain and need fiscal resources.

For the UK, the deficit has been financed for decades without crisis because of deep financial markets, a floating exchange rate, borrowing in its own currency and institutional credibility, which suggests the deficit is less pressing than in emerging economies; however, episodes such as 2022 show that confidence can shift quickly.
Global perspective: imbalances require adjustment by both deficit and surplus countries; pressure only on deficit countries tends to depress world demand.
misconceptions: Saying the balance of payments is in deficit. The overall balance of payments always balances; it is the current account that is in deficit or surplus.

Confusing a current account deficit with a budget deficit. One is about transactions with the rest of the world, the other about government spending and taxation, though the twin deficits can be linked.
Placing interest and dividends from abroad in the financial account. Income from assets is primary income in the current account; buying the assets is in the financial account.
Assuming a current account deficit is always bad. It can reflect strong investment, strong growth relative to trading partners, or attractiveness to foreign investors.
Assuming a depreciation will improve the current account immediately. The J-curve shows it usually worsens first.
exam_tips: Data response questions often give BoP components: calculate the balance, convert to % of GDP and identify which component drove the change.
When asked about policies, classify them clearly as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side, and evaluate each against conflicts with other objectives.
Use the AD/AS diagram to show both an expenditure-reducing policy and a supply-side improvement; label shifts and equilibrium points.
For the significance of a deficit, structure evaluation around size, persistence, cause and method of financing.
